title: Trump Announces 'AI Force' and AI Tsar, Calls Safety Warnings a 'Hoax'
summary: President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that the U.S. will form an 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar — a top official to lead AI policy. In a social media post, he said his administration 'will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth' of AI and rejected calls to slow development until better safeguards exist. 'AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP,' Trump wrote. GDP, or gross domestic product, is the total value of everything a country produces. He added that he wants the U.S. to keep leading China in AI. AI is now central to the U.S.-China rivalry, and it's expected to come up when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week. Trump also said his administration would use existing criminal and civil courts to target anyone misusing AI, and he repeated that concerns about AI's dangers are a 'hoax.' But many AI leaders disagree. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google — the companies behind Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini — have reported security breaches and cases where their chatbots were used for 'malicious activity.' Anthropic's CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for industry-wide deceleration, regulation, and independent monitoring of AI models. OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk both said they agree with his recommendations. Altman told a San Francisco conference that Washington has struggled to keep up with the fast-moving technology. 'The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this,' he said. In the UK, a cross-party committee of MPs and peers published a report calling for a new AI bill to address human rights risks, arguing current laws are ill-equipped for AI's rapid growth.
why_it_matters: The rules for AI are being written right now by people who disagree about whether its risks are real, and those choices — over safety testing, competition with China, and who watches the technology — will shape the jobs, tools and information today's teenagers inherit.

background_read: Artificial intelligence became a global race in late 2022, when OpenAI (the American company behind the ChatGPT chatbot) released a tool that could write, code and answer questions — triggering huge investment from Google, Microsoft, Meta and Chinese firms alike.

Governments have struggled to keep up: the European Union passed the world's first broad AI law, the AI Act, in 2024, and the United Kingdom hosted an international AI safety summit at Bletchley Park in 2023 where countries agreed to cooperate on testing the most powerful models.

The United States and China are the two main competitors in the field, and Washington has restricted exports of advanced computer chips to China to slow its progress; Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) is due to meet Xi Jinping (China's president since 2012) — the meeting mentioned in the article.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Google (the companies behind the chatbots Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini) each publish their own safety policies, which is why their leaders' public calls for slower, monitored development sit so awkwardly beside Trump's description of safety warnings as a 'hoax'.

perspectives.description: Trump and his supporters argue that refusing to 'hinder or stifle' AI keeps the United States ahead of China and delivers enormous economic gains — up to a quarter of GDP. An 'AI Force' plus a single AI tsar, they say, gives one clear chain of command instead of scattered agencies, and using existing courts avoids creating new bureaucracy.

AI company leaders and the UK committee say the dangers are not a 'hoax': Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have already reported security breaches and chatbots used for malicious activity. Labelling safety warnings a hoax, critics argue, makes it politically harder to pass the binding rules that current laws — described as ill-equipped — cannot provide.

Historically, transformative technologies have spread faster than the laws written for them — the Industrial Revolution, electricity and the internet all followed this pattern. The added twist here is that AI is a strategic rivalry as well as a safety question, so every country faces the same dilemma: whoever regulates first may simply fall behind.

The next signals to watch are the Trump–Xi meeting and whether Washington moves from announcements to actual funding, staffing and legal authority for its 'AI Force'. In the UK, the question is whether the committee's proposed AI bill becomes law, and whether voluntary company pledges evolve into independent monitoring with real teeth.
